blocks.text: The chapter presents Jehu as carrying out judgment on Ahab’s house and eliminating Baal worship (vv. 28–30), but it immediately adds a limit: he continued the practices associated with Jeroboam’s shrines and did not follow the LORD wholeheartedly (vv. 29–31). The narrative therefore distinguishes between accomplishing the assigned judgment and treating every aspect of Jehu’s rule or methods as exemplary.

An Assyrian monument known as the Black Obelisk includes a caption identifying tribute from Jehu, or from the house of Omri, and depicts submission before the Assyrian king. This does not appear in 2 Kings 9–10, nor does it verify the chapter’s account of Jehu’s coup. It does, however, provide external evidence of a political relationship involving Jehu that this narrative does not describe.
